intro: Every skater's first tricks are small ones. You press the tail and the front wheels lift. You swing the board side to side and it creeps forward. You find the spot where the board balances on two wheels. These moves are the building blocks for almost everything that comes later.

In this unit you will learn the kickturn, the tic-tac and the manual on flat ground. Then you will move to a small ramp. You will learn ramp words, the drop-in, carving, and pumping for speed. Each trick starts with safety gear and a smooth, dry place, with a grown-up nearby.

You will also learn why the tricks work. The board is a lever that turns around its back wheels. Gravity pulls you down a ramp. Friction slows you a little, and your legs can add energy back. By the end, you will be able to explain each trick's steps and the science under it.
bigQuestion: How do small, careful steps and a little science help you learn your first skateboard tricks?

timeline.t: Put on a buckled helmet, wrist guards, pads and flat shoes
Practice falling small on soft grass: get low, slide, roll
Learn the kickturn standing still on grass or carpet
Try kickturns while rolling slowly on smooth, flat ground
Move forward with tic-tacs, small kickturns side to side
Find the balance point and hold a manual on the back wheels
On a small ramp with a coach, practice knee slides and rolling fakie
Set up on the coping and drop in, chest over the front foot
Carve long, smooth turns on your toe side and heel side
Pump a small halfpipe to gain speed without pushing

words.d: the back end of the deck, which curves up
the front end of the deck, which also curves up
a turn made by pressing the tail, lifting the front wheels, and swinging the board on its back wheels
small kickturns from side to side, done one after another to move forward
rolling on only the back wheels, with the nose up and the tail not touching
a bar that turns around one point; pushing one end moves the other end
the point a lever turns around; on a skateboard, the back wheels
the metal pipe or edge along the top of a ramp
the curved part of a ramp between the flat ground and the top
starting a ramp by rolling down it from the top
a long, smooth turn made by leaning on your toes or heels while you roll
to bend and straighten your legs at the right times on a ramp to gain speed

test.q: Which gear helps prevent one of the most common skateboarding injuries?
test.why: Wrist injuries are among the most common, and wrist guards help prevent them.

test.q: Which foot presses the tail in a kickturn?
test.why: The ball of the back foot presses the tail.

test.q: A goofy rider and a regular rider both learn a kickturn. Which is true?
choices: Both are normal, so steps say front foot and back foot
Goofy riders use the nose instead
test.why: Both stances are normal, so steps use front foot and back foot.

test.q: What happens when you press the tail far too hard?
choices: The board can shoot out from under you
test.why: Too much weight on the tail sends the board out ahead.

test.q: What moves the board forward in a tic-tac?
choices: Small kickturns from side to side
test.why: Small side-to-side kickturns creep the board forward.

test.q: In a manual, what keeps you on the back wheels without the tail scraping?
choices: Leaning as far back as possible
test.why: At the balance point the board stays steady without tipping.

test.q: When you press the tail, the board turns around which part?
test.why: The back wheels are the fulcrum of the lever.

test.q: What did Larry Stevenson's 1971 patent cover?
test.why: Larry Stevenson's kicktail patent was granted in 1971.

test.q: Why does practice work better in short sessions on many days?
choices: Long days wear out the board
Each try teaches muscles and brain, and rest and sleep help store the skill
It does not matter how you practice
test.why: Many short practices plus rest help the body and brain learn.

test.q: What is the curved part of a ramp called?
test.why: The transition is the curve between the flat ground and the top.

test.q: Rolling backward in your normal stance is called what?
test.why: Fakie means rolling backward while keeping your normal stance.

test.q: Where should your chest be during a drop-in?
test.why: Leaning your chest over the front foot keeps your weight over the board.

test.q: You press your toes while rolling. What happens?
choices: The board turns toward the heel side
The board turns toward the toe side
test.why: Pressing your toes tilts the trucks and turns the board toward the toe side.

test.q: On a halfpipe, why does each trip go lower if you do not pump?
choices: Friction turns a little energy into heat and sound
Stored energy turns into more height
test.why: Friction takes a little energy away on every trip.

test.q: When do you stand up tall while pumping?
choices: At the very top of the wall
As you roll through the curve
test.why: Standing up and pressing into the curve adds energy from your legs.

write.prompt: Teach a younger student either the kickturn or the drop-in. Explain the safety gear, where each foot goes, the steps in order, one common problem and its fix, and the science that makes it work (the tail as a lever, or gravity pulling the board down the ramp).
tips: Say front foot and back foot, not left and right.
Use First, Next, Then and Last for the steps.
Name one problem, like pressing too hard or leaning back, and how to fix it.
Use one science word from the unit, such as lever, fulcrum, gravity or friction.

title: First Tricks

chapters.title: Kickturns, Tic-Tacs and Manuals
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a small, gentle press on the tail turn into your first real tricks?

story.title: Too Hard, Then Just Right
story.kicker: A beginner learns that the tail needs a gentle press, not a stomp.
paragraphs: Maya buckles her helmet and checks the strap under her chin. One finger fits, no more. Her wrist guards are snug. Her dad sits on a bench at the edge of the empty school blacktop. The ground is smooth and dry, and no cars come near.

Maya has watched videos of kickturns. The rider presses the back of the board, the front wheels lift, and the board swings around. It looks easy. She puts her back foot on the tail and stomps down hard.
The board shoots forward out from under her. Maya drops low and lands on her knee pads. She slides a little and stops. Her hands stay tucked in. Nothing hurts, but her heart is pounding.
Her dad brings the board back. "What happened?" he asks. Maya thinks. "I pushed way too hard," she says. "All my weight went to the back. The board had nowhere to go but out."

This time she stands on the board in the grass first. She presses the tail gently, like pressing a doorbell. The front wheels rise just a few centimeters. She turns her shoulders, and the board turns with her. She sets the wheels down softly and grins.
story.think: Why did a gentle press work better for Maya than a hard stomp?

lessons.title: Gear That Fits
lessons.mainIdea: A buckled helmet that fits, wrist guards, pads and flat shoes protect you while you learn new tricks.
reading: Before any trick, put on a *helmet*. It should sit low on your forehead, not tipped back. Buckle the strap every time. Only about one finger should fit between the strap and your chin. A helmet that wobbles cannot do its job.

Next come *wrist guards*. When people fall, they often reach out with their hands. That is why wrist injuries are among the most common skateboarding injuries. Wrist guards have hard plastic pieces that help keep the wrist from bending too far.

Knee pads and elbow pads let you slide when you fall instead of scraping. Wear flat shoes with flat rubber bottoms. Flat soles grip the board. Open sandals, boots with heels, and bare feet are not safe on a board.

words.d: a hard hat with soft padding inside that protects your head; buckle it every time
pads with hard plastic pieces that protect your wrists if you fall

look.title: The Gear Check
look.text: Picture a skater getting ready. Helmet low on the forehead, strap buckled, one finger under the chin strap. Wrist guards on both hands. Pads on both knees and both elbows. Shoes with flat rubber soles, laces tied tight.
look.prompt: Check your own gear from head to toe. What is on, and what is missing?

check.q: How should a helmet strap fit?
choices: Buckled, with about one finger of space under the chin
So loose the helmet tips back
check.why: A buckled strap with about one finger of space keeps the helmet in place.

check.q: Why are wrist guards important?
choices: They make the board go faster
Wrist injuries are among the most common skateboarding injuries
check.why: People often fall onto their hands, so wrists get hurt a lot. Wrist guards help prevent that.

check.q: Which shoes are best for skating?
choices: Flat shoes with flat rubber soles
check.why: Flat rubber soles grip the board and protect your feet.

lessons.title: A Good Practice Spot
lessons.mainIdea: Learn on ground that is smooth, dry and flat, far from cars, with a grown-up nearby.
reading: Small wheels stop fast when they hit a pebble or a crack. A smooth, flat surface lets the wheels roll evenly. Good spots include an empty blacktop, a quiet basketball court, or the flat part of a skatepark. Sweep away sticks and stones first.

Water makes the ground slippery and can ruin the small metal parts inside the wheels. So skate only when the ground is dry. Stay far from streets, driveways and parking lots, where cars move. A hill is never a place to learn.

Doctors say children ages 6 to 10 should have a grown-up watching when they skate. Children under 5 should not ride skateboards at all. A grown-up can help you choose a safe spot and can help if you fall.

words.d: the top layer of the ground you ride on, such as blacktop or concrete
to watch and help someone so they stay safe

look.title: What Children's Doctors Advise
look.text: Children younger than 5 should not ride skateboards. Children from 6 to 10 should ride only with an adult watching them.
look.cite: American Academy of Pediatrics, skateboard safety advice
look.prompt: How old are you? What does this advice mean for you?

check.q: Which place is best for learning a trick?
choices: A hill with a street at the bottom
A smooth, dry, empty basketball court
check.why: A smooth, dry, flat place away from cars lets the wheels roll evenly and safely.

check.q: Why should you not skate on wet ground?
choices: Wet ground is slippery and water can harm parts in the wheels
Wet ground makes the board heavier
check.why: Water makes the ground slippery and can ruin the small metal parts inside the wheels.

check.q: What do children's doctors say about skaters ages 6 to 10?
choices: They should have a grown-up watching
They should only skate on hills
check.why: The American Academy of Pediatrics advises that children 6 to 10 be supervised by an adult.

lessons.title: How to Fall Small
lessons.mainIdea: Falling is part of learning; crouch low, land on your pads, and roll instead of catching yourself with straight arms.
reading: Every skater falls, even the best ones. Falling is part of learning. What matters is falling small. When you feel the board slipping, bend your knees and get low. A low fall is a short fall.

Next, land on the parts with pads. Drop to your knee pads and *slide* forward. Or tuck your chin and *roll* onto your shoulder and side. Keep your arms bent and close to your body. Never catch yourself with stiff, straight arms. Locked arms send the whole force into your wrists.

Practice falling on grass before you need it. Stand up, crouch, and drop to your knees. Then try rolling sideways. If a fall makes you scared, that is normal. Take a breath and try a smaller step next.

words.d: in a fall, to land on your knee pads and skid forward to a stop
in a fall, to tuck and turn your body so it lands on your shoulder and side

look.title: Two Ways to Fall
look.text: Skater one feels the board slip, stands tall, and shoots both arms out straight. Skater two feels the board slip, bends low, drops onto knee pads, and slides with arms bent close to the chest.
look.prompt: Which skater falls small? Practice skater two's fall on soft grass.

check.q: What is the first thing to do when the board slips?
choices: Stand up as tall as you can
Bend your knees and get low
check.why: Getting low makes the fall shorter and softer.

check.q: Why should you never catch yourself with locked straight arms?
choices: The whole force goes into your wrists
It makes the board roll away
check.why: Stiff arms send the force of the fall straight into the wrists.

check.q: Where is a good place to practice falling?
check.why: Soft grass is a gentle place to practice sliding and rolling.

lessons.title: Tail, Nose and Bolts
lessons.mainIdea: Knowing the tail, the nose, the bolts and your front and back foot helps you follow any trick's steps.
reading: The flat board you stand on is the deck. The back end curves up. That end is the *tail*. The front end curves up too. That end is the *nose*. On many boards the nose is a little longer than the tail.
Look at the top of the deck. You will see four small screw heads near each end. These are the *bolts*. They hold the trucks and wheels to the deck. Bolts show you where to put your feet.

Some riders stand with the left foot forward. That is called regular. Others put the right foot forward. That is called goofy. Both are normal. So trick steps say front foot and back foot. Your back foot works the tail.

words.d: the back end of the deck, which curves up
the front end of the deck, which also curves up
the screws on top of the deck that hold the trucks on; they show where your feet go

look.title: Find the Parts
look.text: Set a board on the carpet. Touch the back end that curves up: the tail. Touch the front end: the nose. Count the four bolts near the tail and the four near the nose. Stand on it the way that feels natural. Which foot is in front?
look.prompt: Are you regular or goofy? Say which foot is your front foot.

check.q: What is the tail of a skateboard?
choices: The back end of the deck that curves up
The front end of the deck
check.why: The tail is the back end of the deck, and it curves up.

check.q: A rider stands with the right foot forward. What is that stance called?
check.why: Goofy means riding with the right foot forward. Both goofy and regular are normal.

check.q: Why do trick steps say front foot and back foot instead of left and right?
choices: Because left and right are hard words
Because riders can be regular or goofy
Because boards have no left side
Because only goofy riders do tricks
check.why: Regular riders lead with the left foot and goofy riders with the right, so front and back works for everyone.

lessons.title: Kickturn on the Grass
lessons.mainIdea: A kickturn means pressing the tail to lift the front wheels, turning, and setting the wheels back down.
reading: A *kickturn* is a turn on the back wheels. Start on grass or carpet so the board cannot roll. First, put the ball of your back foot on the tail. Put your front foot just behind the front bolts. Bend your knees.

Next, press the tail down gently. The front wheels lift off the ground. Lift them only a little, about the height of your shoe sole. Then turn your head and shoulders the way you want to go. Your hips and feet follow, and the board pivots on its back wheels.

Last, let the front wheels down softly. Your weight goes back to the middle of the board. Try a small quarter turn first. Then turn a little farther each time. Practice turning both toward your toes and toward your heels.

words.d: a turn made by pressing the tail, lifting the front wheels, and swinging the board on its back wheels
to turn around one point that stays in place

look.title: Kickturn, Step by Step
look.text: Step 1: Back foot on the tail, front foot behind the front bolts. Step 2: Bend your knees. Step 3: Press the tail gently. Step 4: Turn head and shoulders. Step 5: The board pivots on its back wheels. Step 6: Set the front wheels down softly.
look.prompt: On grass, act out each step slowly. Which step needs the gentlest touch?

check.q: Where does the back foot go for a kickturn?
choices: In the middle of the board
check.why: The ball of the back foot goes on the tail so it can press the tail down.

check.q: What leads the turn in a kickturn?
check.why: You turn your head and shoulders first, and your hips, feet and board follow.

check.q: Why start kickturns on grass or carpet?
choices: The board cannot roll away while you learn
Carpet makes the tail lift higher
Grass is the only legal place
check.why: On grass or carpet the board stays still, so you can learn the motion safely.

lessons.title: Kickturns While Rolling
lessons.mainIdea: Once kickturns feel easy standing still, try them while rolling slowly, and keep the tail press gentle.
reading: When kickturns feel easy on grass, move to smooth, flat ground. Have a grown-up nearby. Give one small push and roll slowly. Place your feet the same way as before. Then press, turn and set down.

One common problem is pressing the tail too hard. The front wheels fly up and the board shoots out. The fix is a softer press, just enough to lift the wheels a little. Another problem is the front foot too far forward. Then the tail will not go down. Slide the front foot back toward the middle.

Moving makes a kickturn feel different. The board wants to keep rolling straight. So keep your knees bent and your weight centered over the board. Start with quarter turns. Later try a half turn, so you roll back the other way.

words.d: with your weight balanced over the middle of the board
turning one fourth of the way around, like turning from facing a wall to facing the next wall

look.title: Problem and Fix
look.text: Problem: the board shoots out. Fix: press the tail more gently. Problem: the tail will not go down. Fix: move the front foot back from the nose. Problem: the board spins too far. Fix: turn your shoulders a smaller amount.
look.prompt: Which problem has happened to you? Try its fix three times.

check.q: What usually happens if you press the tail too hard?
choices: The board shoots out from under you
check.why: Too much weight on the tail sends the front wheels up high and the board shoots out.

check.q: The tail will not go down. What is a good fix?
choices: Move the front foot farther onto the nose
Move the front foot back toward the middle
check.why: A front foot too far forward holds the nose down. Sliding it back lets the tail drop.

check.q: What should you do before kickturning while rolling?
choices: Learn kickturns standing still on grass first
Go as fast as you can
check.why: Learning still on grass first, then rolling slowly, is the safe order.

lessons.title: Tic-Tac to Move Forward
lessons.mainIdea: A tic-tac is a string of small kickturns from side to side that moves the board forward without pushing.
reading: A *tic-tac* uses small kickturns to move forward. Stand with your feet in kickturn position on flat ground. Press the tail just enough to lift the front wheels a little. Swing the nose a small way toward your toes. Set it down.

Next, lift the front wheels again. Swing the nose a small way toward your heels. Set it down. Then go back toward your toes. Each small swing moves the board forward a bit. The name comes from the tick-tock sound and motion.

Your shoulders and arms do a lot of the work. Twist your upper body one way, and the board swings the other way. Keep the swings small and even. Big swings make the board zigzag. Tic-tacs help you learn to control the tail.

words.d: small kickturns from side to side, done one after another to move forward
the side of the board where your toes point

look.title: Tick, Tock, Forward
look.text: Picture a board on flat ground. Lift the nose, swing it toward the toe side, set it down. Lift the nose, swing it toward the heel side, set it down. Toe side, heel side, toe side. The board creeps forward like a slow pendulum.
look.prompt: Try five tic-tacs in a row. Did you move forward in a straight line?

check.q: What is a tic-tac?
choices: A string of small kickturns from side to side
A way to stop with your foot
check.why: A tic-tac is small kickturns, back and forth, that move the board forward.

check.q: What happens if your tic-tac swings are too big?
check.why: Big swings make the board zigzag instead of creeping forward.

check.q: What helps swing the board in a tic-tac?
choices: Twisting your shoulders and upper body
Pushing with your front foot on the ground
Holding the nose with your hand
check.why: Twisting your upper body one way swings the board the other way.

lessons.title: Balancing on the Back Wheels
lessons.mainIdea: A manual is rolling on only the back wheels, finding the balance point and holding it.
reading: A *manual* is like a wheelie on a bike. You roll on only the back wheels. First, practice on grass. Put your back foot on the tail and your front foot behind the front bolts. Shift your weight back slowly until the front wheels lift. Find the spot where they stay up without the tail touching.

That spot is the *balance point*. Hold your arms out to the sides. Bend your knees a little. Small moves of your hips keep you there. Then let your weight move forward again, and the nose drops back down.

Next, try it rolling slowly on flat ground. If the tail scrapes the ground, you leaned too far back. Ease your weight forward a little. If the front wheels drop fast, you need a bit more weight on the back. Count how long you hold it.

words.d: a trick where you roll on only the back wheels, with the nose up and the tail not touching
the exact spot where your weight keeps the board steady without tipping either way

look.title: Finding the Sweet Spot
look.text: Picture a seesaw with the back wheels as its middle. Too much weight back, and the tail hits the ground. Too much weight forward, and the nose drops. Somewhere in between, the nose floats. Arms out, knees soft, hips making tiny moves.
look.prompt: On grass, how many seconds can you hold the nose up before it drops?

check.q: In a manual, which wheels are touching the ground?
check.why: A manual is rolling on only the back wheels.

check.q: Your tail scrapes the ground in a manual. What should you do?
choices: Ease your weight forward a little
check.why: A scraping tail means you leaned too far back, so move your weight forward a little.

check.q: What is the balance point?
choices: The spot where your weight keeps the board steady
The highest part of the nose
check.why: The balance point is where the board stays steady without tipping.

sections.title: Why It Works and How to Practice

lessons.title: The Tail Is a Lever
lessons.mainIdea: The board works like a lever: press the tail down, the back wheels act as the pivot, and the nose goes up.
reading: A *lever* is a bar that turns around a point. A seesaw is a lever. When you press down on the tail, the board turns around its back wheels. That turning point is called the *fulcrum*. The tail goes down, and the nose goes up.

The tail is short. The rest of the board is long. So a small drop of the tail moves the nose up much farther than the tail moves down. That is why a small, gentle press is all the movement you need. A big stomp lifts the nose much too far.

Early boards were flat, with no tail. Larry Stevenson got a patent for a kicktail in 1971. A kicktail is a tail bent up. It gives your foot a place to press and lifts the nose more easily. Almost every board now has a kicktail and a bent nose.

words.d: a bar that turns around one point; pushing one end moves the other end
the point a lever turns around; on a skateboard, the back wheels
a tail bent upward so your foot can press it

look.title: Boards Change Over Time
look.cite: Skateboarding history; U.S. patent for the kicktail, granted 1971
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first store-made boards and the kicktail patent?

check.q: When you press the tail, what is the fulcrum?
check.why: The board turns around its back wheels, so they are the fulcrum.

check.q: Why does a small press on the tail lift the nose a lot?
choices: The tail is short and the rest of the board is long
The nose is made of lighter wood
The wheels push the nose up
check.why: The nose is much farther from the back wheels than the tail is, so it moves much farther.

check.q: Who got a patent for the kicktail in 1971?
check.why: Larry Stevenson's kicktail patent was granted in 1971.

lessons.title: A Little Every Day
lessons.mainIdea: Short practice on many days builds a trick better than one very long practice.
reading: Your body learns a trick by doing it many times. Each try teaches your muscles and brain a little more. Short practice on many days works better than one very long day. Ten or fifteen minutes is a good start.

Plan each practice. First, warm up by rolling slowly and doing easy kickturns. Next, work on one new skill, like the manual. Then end with something you already do well. Ending on a good try helps you feel ready for next time.

Rest is part of practice too. Tired legs wobble, and wobbly legs fall more. Stop when you feel tired or upset. Sleep also helps your brain store what you practiced. Tomorrow the trick may feel easier.

words.d: doing a skill again and again to get better at it
easy moves at the start that get your body ready

look.title: One Example Practice Week
look.prompt: How many minutes in all does this example week have? Why might Wednesday be zero?

check.q: Which plan helps you learn a trick best?
choices: One very long practice once a month
check.why: Short practice on many days helps the body and brain learn.

check.q: What is a good way to end a practice?
choices: With the hardest trick you cannot do
With something you already do well
By skipping the cool-down and running off
check.why: Ending on a good try helps you feel ready for next time.

check.q: Why is rest part of practice?
choices: Tired legs wobble and fall more, and sleep helps the brain store skills
check.why: Tired legs fall more, and sleep helps your brain store what you practiced.

review.q: What should you always do with your helmet strap?
review.why: A helmet only stays on in a fall if the strap is buckled.

review.q: In a kickturn, what lifts off the ground?
review.why: Pressing the tail lifts the front wheels so the board can pivot on its back wheels.

review.q: Which trick uses small kickturns from side to side to move forward?
review.why: A tic-tac is a string of small kickturns.

review.q: Maya stomped hard on the tail and the board shot out. What would help?
choices: A gentler press on the tail
review.why: A gentle press lifts the nose just enough without sending the board out.

choices: Rolling on only the back wheels
Spinning the board in the air
review.why: A manual is balancing on the back wheels while rolling.

review.q: In the tail-as-lever idea, what goes up when the tail goes down?
review.why: The board turns around the back wheels, so the nose rises as the tail goes down.

review.q: What is the safe order for learning a kickturn?
choices: On a hill first, then flat ground
Still on grass first, then rolling slowly
review.why: Learn standing still on grass first, then try it rolling slowly.

review.q: What is the safest way to fall?
choices: Get low and slide on your knee pads with arms bent
Stay tall and catch yourself with straight arms
Grab the board with your hands
review.why: Falling small means getting low, landing on pads, and keeping arms bent.

chapters.title: Dropping In and Carving
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you go from standing at the top of a ramp to riding it smoothly, without pushing at all?

story.title: The Longest Minute
story.kicker: A rider waits at the top of a small ramp, then finds the courage to lean forward.
paragraphs: Jordan stands on the flat top of a small quarter pipe at the skatepark. The ramp is only about as tall as his waist. From up here it looks much taller. His coach, Ms. Rivera, stands on the ramp below him, ready to hold out a hand.

His tail sits on the metal edge at the top. His back foot holds the board steady. The front of the board sticks out over the curved wall, front wheels in the air. All he has to do is put his front foot down and lean.

He waits. A minute goes by. Then another. Other skaters roll past on the flat ground. Jordan's legs feel shaky. "It is okay to take your time," Ms. Rivera says. "Fear is your body telling you to pay attention."

She reminds him of the plan. "Front foot on the front bolts. Chest over your front foot. Lean more than feels right. Keep your knees bent." Jordan has practiced each part on a smaller ramp. He knows the steps.

He takes a slow breath. He places his front foot on the bolts and pushes his weight forward. The front wheels slap onto the ramp. The board rolls down the curve, and Jordan rides all the way across the flat ground. He turns around, smiling, and walks back up to try again.
story.think: What helped Jordan finally lean forward and drop in?

lessons.title: Words for Ramps
lessons.mainIdea: A ramp has a flat top called the deck, a metal edge called the coping, a curved wall called the transition, and a flat bottom.
reading: A quarter pipe is a ramp shaped like one side of a U. At the top is a flat platform where you stand. Skaters call it the deck, just like the top of a board. Along its front edge runs a metal pipe or bar. That edge is the *coping*.

Below the coping the wall curves down to the ground. The curved part is the *transition*. Skaters often shorten it to tranny. The curve is what lets a board roll smoothly from going down to going across.

At the bottom is the flat ground, called the flat bottom. A halfpipe is two quarter pipes facing each other, joined by flat bottom. On a halfpipe you can ride back and forth from one wall to the other.

words.d: the metal pipe or edge along the top of a ramp
the curved part of a ramp between the flat ground and the top
two curved ramps facing each other, like a U

look.title: Draw a Ramp
look.text: Draw a flat line for the ground. On the right side, draw a curve that rises like the inside of a bowl. At the top of the curve, draw a small circle for the coping. Behind it, draw a short flat line for the deck where a rider stands.
look.prompt: Label the flat bottom, the transition, the coping and the deck on your drawing.

check.q: What is the coping?
choices: The flat ground at the bottom
The metal edge along the top of a ramp
check.why: The coping is the metal pipe or edge at the top of a ramp.

check.q: What do skaters call the curved part of a ramp?
check.why: The curve between the flat ground and the top is the transition.

check.q: What is a halfpipe?
choices: Two quarter pipes facing each other
check.why: A halfpipe is two quarter pipes facing each other, shaped like a U.

lessons.title: Start Small with a Coach
lessons.mainIdea: Learn ramp skills on a small, low ramp with a coach or grown-up nearby and all your pads on.
reading: Ramps add height, and height adds speed. So the first ramp should be small and low. Many skateparks have a little quarter pipe for beginners. Choose a ramp with a smooth curve and no cracks.

Wear your helmet, wrist guards, knee pads and elbow pads. On a ramp, knee pads are extra important. If you fall, you can drop to your knees and slide down the curve. This is called a knee slide. Practice it on the ramp before you try anything else.
Have a coach or a grown-up with you. They can hold your hand for your first tries. Watch which way other skaters are going. Wait your turn so no one rolls into you. Skateparks run on taking turns.

words.d: a safe way to fall on a ramp by dropping onto your knee pads and sliding down
a person who teaches a skill and helps you practice it safely

choices: Height adds speed, so a low ramp is gentler

check.why: A knee slide is a safe ramp fall onto your knee pads.

choices: So no one rolls into anyone else

check.why: Taking turns keeps skaters from crashing into each other.

lessons.title: Rolling Up and Back Down
lessons.mainIdea: Rolling a little way up a ramp and back down backward, called fakie, teaches the feel of the curve.
reading: Before dropping in from the top, learn the ramp from the bottom. Roll slowly toward the ramp across the flat bottom. Keep your knees bent and your weight over the middle of the board. Let the board roll a little way up the curve.

Near the top of your roll, the board slows and stops for a moment. Then gravity pulls it back down. Stay in the same stance and roll down backward. Riding backward in your normal stance is called *fakie*. Keep your eyes looking down the ramp.

Each time, roll a little higher. Your body learns how the curve pushes up on the wheels. If you feel the board wobble, bend your knees more. Rolling fakie on a small ramp is a step toward dropping in.

words.d: rolling backward while standing in your normal stance
the pull that brings everything down toward the ground

look.title: Up, Pause, Back
look.text: Picture a rider rolling slowly toward a small ramp. The board climbs the curve and slows. For one moment it stops. Then it rolls back down, tail first, and out across the flat bottom. The rider never moved her feet.
look.prompt: Where on the ramp is the rider going slowest? Where is she going fastest?

check.q: What is fakie?
choices: Rolling backward in your normal stance
check.why: Fakie means rolling backward while keeping your normal stance.

check.q: What pulls the board back down the ramp after it stops?
check.why: Gravity pulls the board back down the curve.

check.q: The board wobbles as you roll up the ramp. What helps?
check.why: Bent knees help you soak up the curve and stay steady.

lessons.title: Setting Up on the Coping
lessons.mainIdea: To set up a drop-in, the tail sits on the coping and the back foot holds it while the front of the board hangs over the ramp.
reading: A *drop-in* is starting a ramp from the top. First, stand on the deck of the ramp, back from the edge. Set the board so the tail rests on top of the coping. The back wheels sit on the deck side of the coping. The front of the board sticks out over the curve.
Next, put your back foot on the tail. Press down to hold the board still. Now the front wheels float in the air over the ramp. Your front foot stays on the deck for now. You are in the *setup*.

Check the ramp below you. Wait until no one is rolling there. Ask your coach to stand on the ramp and hold out a hand. Take a breath. Your back foot keeps the board locked in place until you are ready.

words.d: starting a ramp by rolling down it from the top
the starting position for a drop-in, with the tail on the coping and the back foot holding it

look.title: The Setup Picture
look.text: Picture the top of a small ramp. The tail rests on the coping. The back wheels sit on the flat deck behind it. The rider's back foot presses the tail. The front wheels hang in the air above the curve. The rider's front foot waits on the deck.
look.prompt: Stand on a board on carpet and act out the setup. Which foot holds the board still?

check.q: In the drop-in setup, where is the tail?
check.why: The tail rests on top of the coping, held there by the back foot.

check.q: Which foot holds the board still in the setup?
check.why: The back foot presses the tail to keep the board locked in place.

check.q: What should you check before dropping in?
choices: That no one is rolling on the ramp below
check.why: Waiting until the ramp below is clear keeps everyone safe.

lessons.title: Lean Forward and Commit
lessons.mainIdea: To drop in, put the front foot on the bolts, lean your chest over it, and commit with bent knees.
reading: From the setup, place your front foot on the front bolts. Keep your back foot on the tail. Now comes the key move. Lean forward and push your weight onto your front foot. The front wheels drop onto the ramp.

Lean your chest out over your front foot, toward the bottom of the ramp. It will feel like too much. That is right. Keep both knees bent so you can soak up the curve. Let both feet press the board flat onto the ramp. Look ahead at the flat bottom, not at your feet.

To *commit* means to go all the way once you start. Halfway leaning is what causes falls. Ride down the curve and across the flat bottom. Then stop or roll up the other side. With a coach's hand, the first tries feel much safer.

words.d: to go all the way with a move once you start it
the bolts near the nose, where the front foot goes for a drop-in

look.title: Drop-In, Step by Step
look.text: Step 1: Tail on the coping, back foot holding it. Step 2: Front foot on the front bolts. Step 3: Lean your chest over your front foot. Step 4: Front wheels drop onto the ramp. Step 5: Knees bent, eyes ahead. Step 6: Ride across the flat bottom.
look.prompt: Which step do you think feels scariest? How could you practice just that step?

check.q: Where does the front foot go for a drop-in?
check.why: The front foot goes on the front bolts before you lean in.

check.q: What does commit mean in a drop-in?
choices: To go all the way once you start
check.why: Committing means going all the way. Leaning only halfway causes falls.

check.q: Where should you look as you drop in?
check.why: Looking ahead helps your body stay over the board.

lessons.title: Why Leaning Back Slips Out
lessons.mainIdea: Leaning back on a drop-in leaves your weight behind the board, so the board slips out ahead of you.
reading: Many new riders lean back on their first drop-in. It feels safer to keep your body away from the slope. But the board does not wait. Gravity pulls it down the ramp right away. If your weight is back, the board rolls out ahead of you.
Then your feet go forward and your body falls back. You land on your back or bottom. This is a very common drop-in fall. It happens because your weight was not over the board.

The fix is to lean forward, with your chest over your front foot. Your body should stay at a right angle to the ramp, like a pole stuck straight into it. Then your weight stays over the wheels and rides down with the board. If you do fall, try to drop to your knees and slide.

words.d: when the board rolls away ahead of your body and you fall
to tilt your body in one direction

look.title: Two Drop-Ins
look.text: Rider one leans back, away from the ramp. The front wheels touch, the board rolls down, and the rider is left behind. Rider two leans chest over the front foot. Her body sticks out from the ramp at a right angle. She and the board roll down together.
look.prompt: Act out both riders on carpet. Where is each rider's weight?

check.q: What usually happens if you lean back on a drop-in?
choices: You go faster and stay on
The board slips out ahead of you
check.why: When your weight is back, gravity pulls the board down the ramp without you.

check.q: How should your body sit on the ramp during a drop-in?
choices: At a right angle to the ramp, chest over the front foot
Standing straight up and down like on flat ground
check.why: Staying at a right angle to the ramp keeps your weight over the wheels.

check.q: What pulls the board down the ramp as soon as the front wheels touch?
check.why: Gravity pulls the board down the slope right away.

lessons.title: When You Feel Scared
lessons.mainIdea: Fear is a normal signal, and breaking a trick into smaller steps helps you get ready.
reading: Most skaters feel scared before their first drop-in. Your heart beats fast. Your legs may shake. This is your body telling you to pay attention. It does not mean you cannot do it.

Break the trick into smaller steps. Practice the setup without dropping in. Practice knee slides on the ramp. Roll fakie higher and higher. Try your first drop-in on the smallest ramp you can find, with a coach holding your hand.
Take slow, deep breaths before you go. Say the steps out loud: front foot, lean, knees bent. It is fine to wait, and it is fine to come back another day. Every skater learns at their own pace.

words.d: a strong feeling that warns you to be careful
one small part of a bigger skill, practiced on its own

look.title: A Ladder of Steps
look.text: Picture a ladder. Bottom rung: stand in the setup on carpet. Next rung: knee slides on a small ramp. Next: roll fakie halfway up. Next: hold the setup at the top of the small ramp. Top rung: drop in with a coach's hand.
look.prompt: Which rung are you on now? What is the next rung for you?

check.q: What does fear before a drop-in mean?
choices: Your body is telling you to pay attention
check.why: Fear is a normal signal to pay attention. It does not mean you cannot do it.

check.q: Which is a good small step toward a drop-in?
choices: Practicing knee slides on a small ramp
check.why: Knee slides are one small step that gets you ready.

check.q: What can you say out loud before you drop in?
check.why: Saying the real steps helps your body remember them.

lessons.title: Toe Side and Heel Side
lessons.mainIdea: Pressing your toes turns the board toward the toe side; pressing your heels turns it toward the heel side.
reading: You can steer a board without lifting any wheels. Press down with your toes, and the deck tilts. The board turns toward your toe side. Press down with your heels, and the board turns toward your *heel side*.

This works because of the trucks. When the deck tilts, the trucks tip and point the wheels in a new direction. Inside each truck are rubber rings called *bushings*. They squish when you lean, then push the board back to level.
Soft wheels grip the ground well in turns. Wheel softness is measured on a scale called durometer A. Lower numbers are softer. Soft wheels are good for cruising and carving on rough ground.

words.d: the side of the board behind your heels
rubber rings inside the trucks that squish when you lean and help you turn
the metal parts under the deck that hold the wheels and let the board turn

look.prompt: Which wheel is softest? Which would grip best on rough ground?

check.why: Pressing your toes tilts the deck and turns the board toward the toe side.

check.q: On the durometer A scale, what does a lower number mean?
check.why: Lower durometer A numbers mean softer wheels.

lessons.title: Long, Smooth Carves
lessons.mainIdea: A carve is a long, smooth turn made by leaning on your toes or heels while you roll.
reading: A *carve* is a long, curving turn. It looks like the letter S drawn on the ground. Start on smooth, flat ground with a grown-up nearby. Push to a slow, steady speed. Put your feet over the bolts with your knees bent.

First, look where you want to go. Turn your head and shoulders that way. Then press gently on your toes for a toe side carve. Hold the lean through the whole turn. Next, shift to your heels for a heel side carve. Linking them makes the S.

A common problem is leaning too hard and too fast. The board turns sharply and you may tip. Lean a little at a time instead. Another problem is stiff legs. Keep your knees soft so your body can move with the board.

words.d: a long, smooth turn made by leaning on your toes or heels while you roll
to join two moves one right after the other

look.title: Draw an S
look.text: Picture chalk lines on a playground. A rider rolls slowly, leans on her toes, and the board curves one way. She shifts to her heels, and it curves the other way. Her wheels leave a long, smooth S. Her shoulders turned first each time.

check.q: What is a carve?
choices: A long, smooth turn made by leaning
check.why: A carve is a long, smooth turn done by leaning on toes or heels.

check.q: What should you do first when you start a carve?

check.why: Looking and turning your shoulders first leads the board into the turn.

check.q: You lean too hard and almost tip. What is the fix?

lessons.title: How to Pump a Ramp
lessons.mainIdea: Pumping means crouching high on the wall and standing up through the curve, which adds speed without pushing.
reading: On a halfpipe you cannot push with your foot. Instead, you *pump*. Pumping means bending and straightening your legs at the right times. Start by rolling back and forth on a small halfpipe, going a little way up each wall.

Near the top of each wall, bend low in a crouch. As you roll down into the curve, push your legs down and stand up tall. Press into the ramp through the bottom of the curve. Then crouch again as you roll up the next wall.

Crouch high, stand in the curve, crouch high again. Each time you do it right, you roll a little higher. If you stand up too early or too late, nothing changes. Watch a skilled rider and notice when their knees bend and straighten.

words.d: to bend and straighten your legs at the right times on a ramp to gain speed
to bend your knees low, close to the board

look.title: Crouch, Stand, Crouch

choices: Pushing with your foot on the ramp

check.why: Pumping is bending and straightening your legs at the right times.

check.q: When should you stand up tall while pumping?
choices: At the top of the wall
As you roll through the curve
check.why: You stand up and press into the ramp through the bottom of the curve.

check.q: When should you crouch while pumping?
choices: Near the top of each wall
In the middle of the flat bottom only
check.why: You crouch low near the top of each wall, then stand in the curve.

lessons.title: Why Pumping Adds Speed
lessons.mainIdea: Friction takes away a little energy on every trip, and pumping puts energy back from your muscles.
reading: When you roll up a ramp, you slow down. Your motion energy turns into stored energy, because you are higher. When you roll back down, the stored energy turns back into motion energy. On a halfpipe, the two keep trading back and forth.

If that were all, you would roll back and forth forever. But *friction* takes a little energy away on every trip. The wheels rub the ramp, and the bearings rub inside. Some energy becomes heat and sound. So without pumping, each trip goes a little lower.

Pumping puts energy back. When you stand up in the curve, your legs push hard against the ramp. That push comes from your muscles. It adds a little energy each time. Add more than friction takes, and you roll higher and faster.

words.d: a force that slows things down when two surfaces rub together
energy that something has because it is high up; also called potential energy
energy that something has because it is moving; also called kinetic energy
